# Section A — Reading an implication

## Question 1 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">Tyler TMUA Set D · P2 Q9</span>

::: {.question}
A set of cards has a single letter printed on the front and a single number printed on the back.

Five of these cards are laid on the table so that only one side of each card is visible. The cards show:

$$5 \qquad \text{E} \qquad 7 \qquad \text{F} \qquad 9$$

Lara states that all cards with a vowel on the front have a prime number on the back.

Which cards do you need to turn over in order to check if this statement is true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** all of the cards

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** cards E, 5 and 7

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** card E only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** cards F and 9

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** cards E and 9
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**E — cards E and 9.**

Lara's statement is an implication: **vowel $\Rightarrow$ prime**. It is false in exactly one situation: a
vowel on one side and a non-prime on the other. So turn over a card only if it could be that situation.

| Card | Could it break the rule? | Turn over? |
|---|---|---|
| **E** | It is a vowel, so the back must be prime. | **Yes** |
| **F** | It is not a vowel, so the rule says nothing about it. | No |
| **5**, **7** | They are prime. A consonant or a vowel on the front is fine either way. | No |
| **9** | It is not prime, so a vowel on the front would break the rule. | **Yes** |

Card 9 is the contrapositive at work: not prime $\Rightarrow$ not a vowel. Turning over 5 or 7 would be
testing the converse, which Lara never claimed.
:::

## Question 2 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">Tyler TMUA Set B · P2 Q11</span>

::: {.question}
The fact that $5\times 6=30$ is a counterexample to which of the following statements?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** the product of any two odd integers is odd

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** if the product of two integers is a multiple of $4$ then the integers are not consecutive

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** if the product of two integers is not a multiple of $4$ then the integers are not consecutive

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** any even integer can be written as the product of two even integers
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**C.**

A counterexample to "if $H$ then $K$" must make $H$ **true** and $K$ **false**. Here the integers are $5$ and
$6$, their product is $30$, they are consecutive, and $30$ is not a multiple of $4$.

- **A:** $5$ and $6$ are not both odd, so the hypothesis fails. This pair says nothing about A.
- **B:** the hypothesis needs a multiple of $4$, and $30$ is not one. The pair says nothing about B.
- **C:** the hypothesis "the product is not a multiple of $4$" is true, and the conclusion "not consecutive"
  is false. This is exactly a counterexample.
- **D:** the claim concerns one even integer written as a product of two **even** integers. Writing $30$ as
  $5\times6$ uses an odd factor, so it does not show that $30$ has no such form.

A pair whose hypothesis is false never refutes an implication.
:::

## Question 3 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">Tyler TMUA Set D · P2 Q10</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the set of integers of the form $3^n-2n-1$, where $n$ is a positive integer greater than $1$.

Which of the following statements are necessarily true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** Integers in this set are even **only if** $n$ is odd.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** Integers in this set are always $2$ more or $2$ less than a multiple of $6$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** Integers in this set are always a multiple of $4$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none of them

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** I only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** I and II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** II and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** I and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** I, II and III
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**D — III only.**

First list some values:

| $n$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ | $5$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $3^n-2n-1$ | $4$ | $20$ | $72$ | $232$ |

**I is false.** "Even only if $n$ is odd" means even $\Rightarrow$ $n$ odd. But $n=2$ gives $4$, which is even
while $n$ is even.

**II is false.** $72$ is itself a multiple of $6$, so it is not $2$ away from one.

**III is true.** Split by the parity of $n$ and work modulo $4$. Note that $3\equiv-1$, so $3^n\equiv(-1)^n$.

- $n$ even: $3^n\equiv1$ and $2n\equiv0$, so $3^n-2n-1\equiv1-0-1=0$.
- $n$ odd: $3^n\equiv-1\equiv3$ and $2n\equiv2$, so $3^n-2n-1\equiv3-2-1=0$.

Both cases give a multiple of $4$.
:::

## Question 4 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock A · P2 Q7</span>

::: {.question}
The non-zero real numbers $a,b,c$ and $d$ satisfy $a<b$ and $c<d$.

Which of the following statements are necessarily true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** $\dfrac{1}{a^3}>\dfrac{1}{b^3}$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** $3^{-a}<3^{-b}$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** If $a,b$ are negative, then $ac<bd$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**IV** If $a,b,c,d$ are all negative, then $ac>bd$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none of them

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** II and IV only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** I, II and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** II, III and IV only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** I, II and IV only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** IV only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** I only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**J** III and IV only
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**H — IV only.**

**I is false.** Take $a=-1,\ b=1$. Then $\dfrac1{a^3}=-1$ and $\dfrac1{b^3}=1$, and $-1>1$ is false.

**II is false.** From $a<b$ we get $-a>-b$. Since $3^x$ is increasing, $3^{-a}>3^{-b}$, which is the reverse
of what II claims.

**III is false.** The hypothesis is only about $a$ and $b$, so $c$ and $d$ can be anything allowed. Take
$a=-2,\ b=-1,\ c=-5,\ d=-4$. Then $ac=10$ and $bd=4$, so $ac<bd$ fails.

**IV is true.** All four are negative, so compare sizes:

- $a<b<0$ gives $|a|>|b|$.
- $c<d<0$ gives $|c|>|d|$.

Multiplying two larger positive sizes gives $|a||c|>|b||d|$. Each product of two negatives is positive, so
$ac=|a||c|$ and $bd=|b||d|$. Hence $ac>bd$.
:::

## Question 5 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2021 · P2 Q12</span>

::: {.question}
Which of the following statements about polynomials $\mathrm f$ and $\mathrm g$ is/are true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** If $\mathrm f(x)\ge\mathrm g(x)$ for all $x\ge0$, then $\displaystyle\int_0^x\mathrm f(t)\,dt\ge\int_0^x\mathrm g(t)\,dt$ for all $x\ge0$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** If $\mathrm f(x)\ge\mathrm g(x)$ for all $x\ge0$, then $\mathrm f'(x)\ge\mathrm g'(x)$ for all $x\ge0$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** If $\mathrm f'(x)\ge\mathrm g'(x)$ for all $x\ge0$, then $\mathrm f(x)\ge\mathrm g(x)$ for all $x\ge0$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none of them

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** I only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** I and II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** I and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** II and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** I, II and III
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**B — I only.**

**I is true.** Subtract the two integrals:

$$\int_0^x\mathrm f(t)\,dt-\int_0^x\mathrm g(t)\,dt=\int_0^x\big(\mathrm f(t)-\mathrm g(t)\big)\,dt .$$

The integrand is never negative on $[0,x]$, so the integral is never negative.

**II is false.** Take $\mathrm f(x)=(x-1)^2$ and $\mathrm g(x)=0$, shown below. Then $\mathrm f\ge\mathrm g$
everywhere, but $\mathrm f'(0)=-2<0=\mathrm g'(0)$. Being above a graph says nothing about being steeper.

```{python}
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x=np.linspace(-0.3,2.4,300); fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(4.8,3.0))
ax.plot(x,(x-1)**2,color='#1f77b4',lw=2,label='$f(x)=(x-1)^2$'); ax.plot(x,0*x,color='#d62728',lw=2,label='$g(x)=0$')
ax.axhline(0,color='0.3',lw=1); ax.axvline(0,color='0.3',lw=1); ax.spines['top'].set_visible(False); ax.spines['right'].set_visible(False)
ax.set_xlabel('$x$'); ax.set_ylabel('$y$'); ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

**III is false.** Take $\mathrm f(x)=x$ and $\mathrm g(x)=x+1$. Then $\mathrm f'=\mathrm g'=1$, so the
hypothesis holds, but $\mathrm f(x)<\mathrm g(x)$ for every $x$. A derivative cannot see an added constant.

Statements II and III are converse-shaped versions of the same idea, and neither direction is automatic.
:::

## Question 6 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock B · P2 Q18</span>

::: {.question}
Let $f$ and $g$ be polynomials. Consider the following four statements.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** If $f'(x)\ge g'(x)$ for all $x\ge0$ and $f(0)\ge g(0)$, then $f(x)\ge g(x)$ for all $x\ge0$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** If $f(x)\ge g(x)$ for all $x\ge0$, then $\displaystyle\int_0^x t\,f(t)\,dt\ge\int_0^x t\,g(t)\,dt$ for all $x\ge0$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** If $\displaystyle\int_0^x f(t)\,dt\ge\int_0^x g(t)\,dt$ for all $x\ge0$, then $f(x)\ge g(x)$ for all $x\ge0$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**IV** If $\displaystyle\int_0^x f(t)\,dt\ge\int_0^x g(t)\,dt$ for all $x\ge0$, then $\displaystyle\int_0^x t^2f(t)\,dt\ge\int_0^x t^2g(t)\,dt$ for all $x\ge0$.

Which of the statements are true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** None of them

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** I only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** IV only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** I and II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** II and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** I and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** all except I

&nbsp;&nbsp;**J** all except II

&nbsp;&nbsp;**K** all except III

&nbsp;&nbsp;**L** all except IV
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**F — I and II only.**

This extends Question 5. Put $h=f-g$, so every statement is about one polynomial $h$.

**I is true.** $h'\ge0$ means $h$ never decreases on $x\ge0$. Since $h(0)\ge0$, it follows that $h(x)\ge0$.

**II is true.** On $[0,x]$ both $t\ge0$ and $h(t)\ge0$, so $t\,h(t)\ge0$ and its integral is not negative.

**III and IV are both false, and one example breaks both.** Define

$$H(x)=x^2(x-1)^2,\qquad h(x)=H'(x)=4x^3-6x^2+2x .$$

Then $\displaystyle\int_0^x h(t)\,dt=H(x)\ge0$ for all $x\ge0$, so the hypothesis of III and IV holds with
$g=0$ and $f=h$.

- **III fails:** $h(x)=2x(x-1)(2x-1)$ is negative on $\tfrac12<x<1$. For example, $h\!\left(\tfrac34\right)=-\tfrac3{16}$.
- **IV fails at $x=1$:**

$$\int_0^1t^2h(t)\,dt=\int_0^1\left(4t^5-6t^4+2t^3\right)dt=\frac23-\frac65+\frac12=-\frac1{30}<0 .$$
:::

# Section B — "Exactly one is true"

## Question 7 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">Tyler TMUA Set A · P2 Q4</span>

::: {.question}
Five sealed jars, labelled A, B, C, D and E, each contain the same (non-zero) number of £1 coins.

The following statements are attached to the jars:

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** This jar contains less than £4

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** This jar contains £5 or £6

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** This jar contains £1 or £6

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** This jar contains more than £3 and less than £6

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** This jar contains £2 or £3

Exactly one of the jars has a true statement attached to it. Which jar is it?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**D.**

All the jars hold the same amount $n$, so the five labels are five claims about one number. Count how many
are true for each $n$.

| $n$ | true labels | how many |
|---|---|---|
| $1$ | A, C | $2$ |
| $2$ | A, E | $2$ |
| $3$ | A, E | $2$ |
| $4$ | D | **$1$** |
| $5$ | B, D | $2$ |
| $6$ | B, C | $2$ |
| $7$ or more | none | $0$ |

Only $n=4$ gives exactly one true label, and that label is D. Note the two connectives: *or* in B, C and E
needs one side, and *and* in D needs both.
:::

---

## Question 8 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock C · P2 Q7</span>

::: {.question}
Six sealed black bags are labelled $P,Q,R,S,T$ and $U$. Each bag contains the same number of balls. This number is a non-zero whole number from $3$ to $8$ inclusive.

Each bag has a label with a statement written on it. The statement may be true or false.

&nbsp;&nbsp;Bag $P$: "The number of balls in this bag is a multiple of $3$."

&nbsp;&nbsp;Bag $Q$: "The number of balls in this bag is even."

&nbsp;&nbsp;Bag $R$: "The number of balls in this bag is prime."

&nbsp;&nbsp;Bag $S$: "The number of balls in this bag is at most $4$."

&nbsp;&nbsp;Bag $T$: "The number of balls in this bag is at least $7$."

&nbsp;&nbsp;Bag $U$: "The number of balls in this bag is a perfect square."

Given that exactly one of the six statements is true, which bag has the true statement on its label?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $P$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** $Q$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** $R$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** $S$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** $T$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** $U$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**C — bag $R$.**

There are only six possible values, so tabulate them.

| $n$ | true labels | how many |
|---|---|---|
| $3$ | $P,R,S$ | $3$ |
| $4$ | $Q,S,U$ | $3$ |
| $5$ | $R$ | **$1$** |
| $6$ | $P,Q$ | $2$ |
| $7$ | $R,T$ | $2$ |
| $8$ | $Q,T$ | $2$ |

So $n=5$, and the only true label is the one on bag $R$.
:::

## Question 9 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock E · P2 Q3</span>

::: {.question}
A real number $x$ is such that **exactly one** of the following six statements is true.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** $x^2<9$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** $|x-1|<1$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** $x,\ 2,\ 4$ are the first three terms of a geometric sequence with positive common ratio

&nbsp;&nbsp;**IV** $\log_2(x+1)$ is defined and less than $1$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**V** $x$ is a positive solution of $u^2-3u+2=0$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**VI** the circle $X^2+Y^2=1$ meets the line $X=x$ in two distinct points

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** I

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** II

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** III

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** IV

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** V

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** VI
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**A — statement I.**

Do not look for $x$. Instead, translate each of II–VI into a range for $x$.

| Statement | Means |
|---|---|
| **II** | $0<x<2$ |
| **III** | the common ratio is $2$, so $x=1$ |
| **IV** | $0<x+1<2$, so $-1<x<1$ |
| **V** | $(u-1)(u-2)=0$, so $x=1$ or $x=2$ |
| **VI** | $-1<x<1$ |

Every one of these ranges lies inside $-3<x<3$, which is statement I. So **each of II–VI implies I**.

If any of II–VI were true, I would be true as well, and that would make two true statements. So none of them
can be the single true statement, which leaves I.

It really can happen: $x=\tfrac52$ makes I true and all the others false.
:::

---

## Question 10 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">Tyler TMUA Set B · P2 Q7</span>

::: {.question}
The real numbers $a$ and $b$ are such that **exactly one** of the following statements is true.

Which is the true statement?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $a\ge0$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** $a<b$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** $a^2>b^2$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** $\lvert a\rvert\le\lvert b\rvert$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**D.**

**Step 1 — spot the complementary pair.** $a^2>b^2$ means the same as $|a|>|b|$, which is exactly the negation
of $|a|\le|b|$. So **C and D are opposites: exactly one of them is always true.**

**Step 2 — use up the "exactly one".** The one true statement must therefore be C or D. So A and B are both
false, which gives

$$a<0\qquad\text{and}\qquad a\ge b .$$

**Step 3 — decide between C and D.** Together these give $b\le a<0$. Both numbers are negative and $b$ is at
least as far from zero, so $|b|\ge|a|$. That is statement D.

**Check:** $a=-1,\ b=-2$ makes A false, B false, C false ($1>4$ fails) and D true.
:::

---

## Question 11 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock D · P2 Q19</span>

::: {.question}
Let $f$ be a function defined on the real numbers. Consider the following seven statements, each intended to hold for all real values of $a$:

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(1)** $f(a)>0$ if $a>0$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(2)** $a>0$ is necessary for $f(a)>0$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(3)** $a\le0$ only if $f(a)\le0$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(4)** If $f(a)\le0$, then $a\le0$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(5)** $f(a)>0$ whenever $a\le0$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(6)** $a>0$ is sufficient for $f(a)>0$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(7)** $f(a)\le0$ is sufficient and necessary for $a>0$.

Given that exactly one of these seven statements is true for the particular function $f$ in question, which one is it?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** Statement (1)

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** Statement (2)

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** Statement (3)

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** Statement (4)

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** Statement (5)

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** Statement (6)

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** Statement (7)
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**E — statement (5).**

Rewrite every statement with the condition on $a$ at the front of the arrow.

| Statement | As written | With $a$ first |
|---|---|---|
| **(1)** | $a>0\Rightarrow f(a)>0$ | $a>0\Rightarrow f(a)>0$ |
| **(2)** | $f(a)>0\Rightarrow a>0$ | $a\le0\Rightarrow f(a)\le0$ |
| **(3)** | $a\le0\Rightarrow f(a)\le0$ | $a\le0\Rightarrow f(a)\le0$ |
| **(4)** | $f(a)\le0\Rightarrow a\le0$ | $a>0\Rightarrow f(a)>0$ |
| **(5)** | $a\le0\Rightarrow f(a)>0$ | $a\le0\Rightarrow f(a)>0$ |
| **(6)** | $a>0\Rightarrow f(a)>0$ | $a>0\Rightarrow f(a)>0$ |
| **(7)** | $f(a)\le0\Leftrightarrow a>0$ | includes $a\le0\Rightarrow f(a)>0$ |

Now eliminate:

- **(1), (4) and (6)** are the same statement, so none of them can be the only true one.
- **(2) and (3)** are the same statement, so neither can be the only true one.
- **(7)** contains (5), since its "necessary" half says $a\le0\Rightarrow f(a)>0$. If (7) were true then (5)
  would be true too.

Only **(5)** is left.
:::

---

## Question 12 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock E · P2 Q12</span>

::: {.question}
Let $f$ be a function. Each of the following is a statement about all real numbers $a$ (for instance, the first reads: for every $a$, if $f(x)>0$ for all $x>a$, then $f(a)<0$). Exactly one of them is true.

Which one is it?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $f(x)>0$ for all $x>a$ **only if** $f(a)<0$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** $f(a)<0$ and $f(x)>0$ for all $x>a$ **cannot both** hold

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** $f(x)>0$ for all $x>a$ is **necessary** for $f(a)<0$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** if $f(a)\ge0$ then $f(x)\le0$ for some $x>a$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** $f(x)>0$ for all $x>a$ **implies** $f(a)\ge0$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** $f(a)\ge0$ **if and only if** $f(x)\le0$ for some $x>a$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** $f(a)<0$ is **sufficient** for there to exist $x>a$ with $f(x)\le0$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**C.**

Name the two halves first:

$$P:\ f(x)>0\text{ for all }x>a,\qquad Q:\ f(a)<0 .$$

Their negations are $\text{not }P$: $f(x)\le0$ for some $x>a$, and $\text{not }Q$: $f(a)\ge0$.

| Option | In arrows | Simplified |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | $P\Rightarrow Q$ | $P\Rightarrow Q$ |
| **B** | not both $Q$ and $P$ | $Q\Rightarrow\text{not }P$ |
| **C** | $Q\Rightarrow P$ | $Q\Rightarrow P$ |
| **D** | $\text{not }Q\Rightarrow\text{not }P$ | $P\Rightarrow Q$ |
| **E** | $P\Rightarrow\text{not }Q$ | $Q\Rightarrow\text{not }P$ |
| **F** | $\text{not }Q\Leftrightarrow\text{not }P$ | $P\Leftrightarrow Q$ |
| **G** | $Q\Rightarrow\text{not }P$ | $Q\Rightarrow\text{not }P$ |

Now eliminate:

- **A and D** are the same statement, so neither can be the only true one.
- **B, E and G** are the same statement, so none of them can be the only true one.
- **F** contains $P\Rightarrow Q$, so if F were true then A would be true too.

Only **C** is left. As in the class questions, you never need to know what $f$ is.
:::

# Section C — "If and only if" and "only if"

## Question 13 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">MAT 2022 · Q1C</span>

::: {.question}
The equation $x^2-4kx+y^2-4y+8=k^3-k$ is the equation of a circle

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** for all real values of $k$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** if and only if either $-4<k<-1$ or $k>1$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** if and only if $k>1$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(d)** if and only if $k<-1$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(e)** if and only if either $-1<k<0$ or $k>1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(b).**

"If and only if" asks for the **exact** set of $k$, with nothing missing and nothing extra.

**Step 1 — complete the square.**

$$(x-2k)^2-4k^2+(y-2)^2-4+8=k^3-k$$

$$(x-2k)^2+(y-2)^2=k^3+4k^2-k-4 .$$

**Step 2 — state the condition.** This is a circle exactly when the right-hand side is positive.

**Step 3 — factorise by grouping.**

$$k^3+4k^2-k-4=k^2(k+4)-(k+4)=(k+4)(k-1)(k+1).$$

**Step 4 — read off the signs.** The cubic has positive leading coefficient and roots $-4,-1,1$.

| range | sign |
|---|---|
| $k<-4$ | $-$ |
| $-4<k<-1$ | $+$ |
| $-1<k<1$ | $-$ |
| $k>1$ | $+$ |

So it is a circle exactly when $-4<k<-1$ or $k>1$. Option (c) is sufficient but misses a whole interval, which
is why it is not an "if and only if".
:::

---

## Question 14 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2023 · P2 Q18</span>

::: {.question}
The equation $x^4+bx^2+c=0$ has four distinct real roots **if and only if** which of the following conditions is satisfied?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $b^2>4c$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** $b^2<4c$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** $c>0$ and $b>2\sqrt c$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** $c>0$ and $b<-2\sqrt c$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** $c<0$ and $b<0$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** $c<0$ and $b>0$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**D.**

Put $u=x^2$, so the equation becomes $u^2+bu+c=0$. Each **positive** root $u$ gives two values $x=\pm\sqrt u$,
while a negative root gives none. So four distinct real $x$ needs **two distinct positive roots $u_1,u_2$.**

Translate that into conditions on the coefficients:

| Requirement | Condition |
|---|---|
| two distinct real roots | $b^2>4c$ |
| product of roots positive, $u_1u_2=c$ | $c>0$ |
| sum of roots positive, $u_1+u_2=-b$ | $b<0$ |

Now combine. With $c>0$, the condition $b^2>4c$ means $b>2\sqrt c$ or $b<-2\sqrt c$. Since $b<0$, only the
second branch survives, and $b<-2\sqrt c$ already forces $b<0$. So the three conditions collapse to

$$c>0\quad\text{and}\quad b<-2\sqrt c .$$

**Why A fails as an "iff".** $b^2>4c$ is necessary but not sufficient: $x^4+3x^2+1=0$ has $b^2=9>4$ and no real
roots at all.
:::

---

## Question 15 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">MAT 2021 · Q1J</span>

::: {.question}
Four distinct real numbers $a,b,c$ and $d$ are used to define four points

$$A=(a,b),\qquad B=(b,c),\qquad C=(c,d),\qquad D=(d,a).$$

The quadrilateral $ABCD$ has all four sides the same length

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** if and only if $(a-b)^2=(c-d)^2$,

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** if and only if $(a-c)^2=(b-d)^2$,

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** if and only if $(a-d)^2=(b-c)^2$,

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(d)** if and only if $a-b+c-d=0$,

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(e)** for no values of $a,b,c,d$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(d).**

**Step 1 — write the four squared lengths.**

$$AB^2=(a-b)^2+(b-c)^2,\qquad BC^2=(b-c)^2+(c-d)^2,$$

$$CD^2=(c-d)^2+(d-a)^2,\qquad DA^2=(d-a)^2+(a-b)^2 .$$

**Step 2 — compare them.** $AB=BC$ gives $(a-b)^2=(c-d)^2$, and $BC=CD$ gives $(b-c)^2=(d-a)^2$. These two
equations also give $CD=DA$, so all four sides are equal **if and only if** both hold.

**Step 3 — remove the squares, using distinctness.** Each equation splits into two cases.

| Equation | Case 1 | Case 2 |
|---|---|---|
| $(a-b)^2=(c-d)^2$ | $a-b=c-d$, so $a+d=b+c$ | $a-b=d-c$, so $a+c=b+d$ |
| $(b-c)^2=(d-a)^2$ | $b-c=d-a$, so $a+b=c+d$ | $b-c=a-d$, so $a+c=b+d$ |

If both equations take Case 1, then $a+d=b+c$ and $a+b=c+d$. Subtracting gives $d-b=b-d$, so $b=d$, which is
not allowed.

If the first takes Case 1 and the second Case 2, then $a+d=b+c$ and $a+c=b+d$. Subtracting gives $d-c=c-d$, so
$c=d$, which is not allowed.

If the first takes Case 2 and the second Case 1, then $a+c=b+d$ and $a+b=c+d$. Subtracting gives $c-b=b-c$, so
$b=c$, which is not allowed.

So **$a+c=b+d$ must hold**, which is $a-b+c-d=0$.

**Step 4 — the other direction.** If $a+c=b+d$, then $a-b=d-c$ and $b-c=a-d$, so both squared equations hold.
Both directions work, which earns the "if and only if".

Option (e) fails because $(a,b,c,d)=(6,5,3,4)$ satisfies $a+c=b+d=9$. Options (a)–(c) fail as "iff": for
example $(a-b)^2=(c-d)^2$ also allows $a+d=b+c$, which does not give equal sides.
:::

## Question 16 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2018 · P2 Q17</span>

::: {.question}
A positive integer is called a *squaresum* **if and only if** it can be written as the sum of the squares of two integers. For example, $61$ and $9$ are both squaresums since $61=5^2+6^2$ and $9=3^2+0^2$.

A prime number is called *awkward* **if and only if** it has a remainder of $3$ when divided by $4$. For example, $23$ is awkward since $23=5\times4+3$.

A (true) theorem due to Fermat states that:

> A positive integer is a squaresum **if and only if** each of its awkward prime factors occurs to an even power in its prime factorisation.

It follows that $5\times23^2$ is a squaresum, since $23$ occurs to the power $2$, but $5\times23^3$ is not, since $23$ occurs to the power $3$.

Which one of the following statements is **not** true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** Every square number is a squaresum.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** If $N$ and $M$ are squaresums, then so is $NM$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** If $NM$ is a squaresum, then $N$ and $M$ are squaresums.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** If $N$ is not a squaresum, then $kN$ is a squaresum for some number $k$ which is a product of awkward primes.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**C.**

Definitions and theorems stated with "if and only if" can be used in **both** directions, and this question
uses both.

**A is true.** $N^2=N^2+0^2$, so it is a sum of two squares directly.

**B is true.** Go from squaresum to prime powers: every awkward prime has an even power in $N$ and in $M$.
Multiplying adds the powers, and even $+$ even is even. Now go back: $NM$ is a squaresum.

**C is false.** Take $N=M=23$. Then $NM=23^2$ has its awkward prime to an even power, so it is a squaresum.
But $23$ on its own has the awkward prime to the power $1$, so it is not. C is the converse of B, and it fails.

**D is true.** Some awkward primes occur in $N$ to odd powers. Let $k$ be the product of exactly those primes.
Multiplying by $k$ raises each of those powers by $1$, so every awkward power in $kN$ is even, and $kN$ is a
squaresum.
:::

---

## Question 17 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2023 · P2 Q20</span>

::: {.question}
Let $f$ be a polynomial with real coefficients.

The integral $I_{p,q}$, where $p<q$, is defined by

$$I_{p,q}=\int_p^q\big(f(x)\big)^2-\big(f(\lvert x\rvert)\big)^2\,dx$$

Which of the following statements must be true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**1** $I_{p,q}=0$ **only if** $0<p$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**2** $f'(x)<0$ for all $x$ **only if** $I_{p,q}<0$ for all $p<q<0$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**3** $I_{p,q}>0$ **only if** $p<0$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none of them

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** 1 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** 2 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** 3 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** 1 and 2 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** 1 and 3 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** 2 and 3 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** 1, 2 and 3
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**D — 3 only.**

**The key fact.** For $x\ge0$, $|x|=x$, so the integrand is $f(x)^2-f(x)^2=0$. Only negative $x$ can contribute.

**Statement 1 means** $I_{p,q}=0\Rightarrow0<p$. This is false. Take $p=0$ and $q=1$: the integrand is zero
throughout, so $I_{0,1}=0$, yet $0<p$ fails.

**Statement 2 means** $f'<0$ everywhere $\Rightarrow I_{p,q}<0$. This is false. Take $f(x)=1-x$, which has
$f'=-1<0$. For $x<0$,

$$f(x)^2-f(|x|)^2=(1-x)^2-(1+x)^2=-4x>0 ,$$

so $I_{p,q}>0$ for $p<q<0$. The graph below shows the two curves on $x<0$.

```{python}
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x=np.linspace(-2,0,200); fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(4.8,3.0))
ax.plot(x,(1-x)**2,color='#1f77b4',lw=2,label='$f(x)^2=(1-x)^2$'); ax.plot(x,(1+x)**2,color='#d62728',lw=2,label='$f(|x|)^2=(1+x)^2$')
ax.axhline(0,color='0.3',lw=1); ax.axvline(0,color='0.3',lw=1); ax.spines['top'].set_visible(False); ax.spines['right'].set_visible(False)
ax.set_xlabel('$x$'); ax.set_ylabel('$y$'); ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

**Statement 3 means** $I_{p,q}>0\Rightarrow p<0$. Use the contrapositive: if $p\ge0$, then $0\le p<q$, so the
integrand is zero on the whole interval and $I_{p,q}=0$, which is not positive. So statement 3 is true.
:::

# Section D — Sufficient and necessary

## Question 18 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2017 · P2 Q19</span>

::: {.question}
Which one of the following is a **sufficient** condition for the equation $x^3-3x^2+a=0$, where $a$ is a constant, to have exactly one real root?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $a>0$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** $a\le0$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** $a\ge4$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** $a<4$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** $\lvert a\rvert>4$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** $\lvert a\rvert\le4$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** $a=\tfrac94$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** $\lvert a\rvert=\tfrac32$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**E.**

"$X$ is sufficient for exactly one root" means $X\Rightarrow$ exactly one root. So every value allowed by $X$
must give exactly one root.

**Step 1 — find the turning points.** With $y=x^3-3x^2+a$, we get $y'=3x^2-6x=3x(x-2)$. So there is a maximum
at $(0,a)$ and a minimum at $(2,a-4)$.

**Step 2 — count the roots.** Changing $a$ only slides the curve up or down. There is exactly one root when
both turning points lie on the same side of the $x$-axis, that is, when $a<0$ or $a>4$.

```{python}
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x=np.linspace(-1.3,3.4,300); fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(4.8,3.2))
for a,c in [(-1,'#1f77b4'),(2,'#7f7f7f'),(5,'#d62728')]:
    ax.plot(x,x**3-3*x**2+a,color=c,lw=2,label=f'$a={a}$')
ax.axhline(0,color='0.3',lw=1); ax.axvline(0,color='0.3',lw=1); ax.spines['top'].set_visible(False); ax.spines['right'].set_visible(False)
ax.set_ylim(-7,8); ax.set_xlabel('$x$'); ax.set_ylabel('$y$'); ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

**Step 3 — test each option against the set "$a<0$ or $a>4$".**

| Option | Verdict |
|---|---|
| **A**, **D**, **F** | allow $a=1$, which gives three roots |
| **B** | allows $a=0$: $x^2(x-3)=0$ has two distinct roots |
| **C** | allows $a=4$: $(x+1)(x-2)^2=0$ has two distinct roots |
| **E** | $a>4$ or $a<-4$: every such value is in the set ✓ |
| **G** | $a=\tfrac94$ lies between $0$ and $4$, so it gives three roots |
| **H** | allows $a=\tfrac32$, which gives three roots |

E does not cover every good value of $a$, and it does not need to. A sufficient condition only has to sit
inside the good set.
:::

---

## Question 19 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2023 · P2 Q5</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the two statements

&nbsp;&nbsp;$R$: $k$ is an integer multiple of $\pi$

&nbsp;&nbsp;$S$: $\displaystyle\int_0^k\sin 2x\,dx=0$

Which of the following statements is true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $R$ is necessary and sufficient for $S$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** $R$ is necessary but not sufficient for $S$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** $R$ is sufficient but not necessary for $S$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** $R$ is not necessary and not sufficient for $S$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**A.**

Evaluate the integral:

$$\int_0^k\sin2x\,dx=\left[-\tfrac12\cos2x\right]_0^k=\tfrac12\left(1-\cos2k\right).$$

So $S$ says $\cos2k=1$. This holds exactly when $2k$ is an integer multiple of $2\pi$, that is, when $k$ is an
integer multiple of $\pi$.

- **Sufficient ($R\Rightarrow S$):** if $k=n\pi$, then $\cos2k=1$, so the integral is $0$.
- **Necessary ($S\Rightarrow R$):** if the integral is $0$, then $\cos2k=1$, so $k=n\pi$.

The graph shows why: the areas above and below the axis cancel only after whole periods of length $\pi$.

```{python}
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x=np.linspace(-0.2,2*np.pi+0.2,400); fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(5.2,2.8))
ax.plot(x,np.sin(2*x),color='#1f77b4',lw=2); ax.fill_between(x,np.sin(2*x),0,where=(x>=0)&(x<=np.pi),color='#1f77b4',alpha=0.2)
ax.axhline(0,color='0.3',lw=1); ax.axvline(0,color='0.3',lw=1); ax.spines['top'].set_visible(False); ax.spines['right'].set_visible(False)
ax.set_xticks([np.pi/2,np.pi,3*np.pi/2,2*np.pi]); ax.set_xticklabels(['$\\pi/2$','$\\pi$','$3\\pi/2$','$2\\pi$']); ax.set_xlabel('$x$'); ax.set_ylabel('$y=\\sin 2x$')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

A similar question with $\sin^2x$ in place of $\sin 2x$ would be different, because that integrand is never
negative. Read the integrand with care.
:::

---

## Question 20 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">Tyler TMUA Set B · P2 Q8</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the following statement about the polynomial $p(x)$, where $a$ and $b$ are real numbers with $a<b$.

$$(*)\quad\text{There exists a number }c\text{ with }a<c<b\text{ such that }p(c)=0$$

Which of the following is true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** The condition $p(a)p(b)<0$ is necessary and sufficient for $(*)$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** The condition $p(a)p(b)<0$ is not necessary and not sufficient for $(*)$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** The condition $p(a)p(b)<0$ is necessary but not sufficient for $(*)$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** The condition $p(a)p(b)<0$ is sufficient but not necessary for $(*)$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**D.**

**Sufficient: yes.** $p(a)p(b)<0$ means $p(a)$ and $p(b)$ have opposite signs. A polynomial has an unbroken
graph, so it must cross the $x$-axis somewhere between $a$ and $b$. That crossing is the required $c$.

**Necessary: no.** To show this, find a case where $(*)$ holds but the condition fails. Take $p(x)=x^2$ with
$a=-1,\ b=1$. Then $c=0$ works, but $p(a)p(b)=1\times1=1$, which is not negative.

```{python}
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x=np.linspace(-1.4,1.4,200); fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(4.8,3.0))
ax.plot(x,x**2,color='#1f77b4',lw=2,label='$p(x)=x^2$'); ax.plot([-1,1],[1,1],'o',color='#d62728',label='$p(a),\\ p(b)$ both positive'); ax.plot([0],[0],'o',color='#2ca02c',label='$c=0$')
ax.axhline(0,color='0.3',lw=1); ax.axvline(0,color='0.3',lw=1); ax.spines['top'].set_visible(False); ax.spines['right'].set_visible(False)
ax.set_xlabel('$x$'); ax.set_ylabel('$y$'); ax.legend(frameon=False,loc='upper center')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The graph can touch the axis, or cross it twice, and still end on the same side at both $a$ and $b$.
:::
